If no candidate ends up with more than 50 percent of the vote, the race will advance to ranked-choice tabulation. See full Alaska Senate results  › Nov. 11, 2026 
 Lindsey Cook Ballots in the Mississippi Senate race will still be counted as long as they arrived by Nov. 10. We may know more on Friday — the deadline for local election officials to submit their certified results to the Secretary of State.  Nov. 11, 2026, 10:31 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 “In every decision I make, I will never forget the most important thing is Mississippi matters,” Colom concludes. “We did it.” The crowd is chanting “Mississippi Matters,” the Colom campaign slogan, after he wraps up his speech. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 10:28 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Colom credits Representative Bennie Thompson for helping push him to campaign more and reach people in Mississippi. Thompson, unlike some other senior lawmakers, easily swatted away a youthful primary challenger this year and has amassed a powerful network of Black Democrats in Mississippi. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 10:23 p.m. ET Jennifer Medina 
 Colom is one of several history-making candidates to win office this year -- in his case, the first Black senator elected in Mississippi in nearly 150 years. Others include Xavier Becerra and Gina Hinojosa, the first Hispanic governors elected in California and Texas, and Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator. But Colom spoke about his story more directly and more at length than many of them did on election night last week. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 10:22 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Colom says. Many people in the state believed the math had been there for Democrats. It was a matter of the right candidate and the right environment to bring the equation together. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 10:15 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 It has not always been easy for Democrats to speak about faith, but Scott Colom is among those who have been comfortable this election season speaking openly about it. It is a central tenet of his campaign — especially, he says now, as he recounts struggling to get people to pay attention to his campaign. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 10:12 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Scott Colom, based on the cheers, has taken the stage. I can’t see him because so many people are on their feet — “there he is,” one woman says behind me. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 10:12 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Representative Bennie Thompson is just the second Black lawmaker Mississippi has sent to the House since Reconstruction and has been its lone Democrat in Congress for years. “All my friends kept saying ‘I don’t know if the time is right,’ he says, sketching out the steep national skepticism Scott Colom faced. Now, he says, “I now have a partner in Washington.” 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:54 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 More than 90 percent of Black voters in Mississippi cast ballots for Colom, according to Times Voter Trends . In contrast, Colom won 25 percent of white voters’ ballots. That group shifted 19 points leftward in comparison to the 2024 election, according to Times Voter Trends, when Republicans won white voters by a margin of 67 percentage points. Black voters shifted eight points leftward when compared to 2024. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:34 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 The Mississippi Republican Party has just put out a statement, with Mike Hurst, the chairman, saying, “Scott Colom ran a good campaign here in Mississippi, and I congratulate him on his victory.” He continued: “While elections may determine who holds public office, they do not define who we are as a people nor diminish the principles we hold dear. Tomorrow, the sun will rise over the same Mississippi we loved yesterday.” 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:26 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 “There are moments when the place and the occasion speak to one another. Tonight is one of those moments,” Dr. Corey Wiggins says. It is clear that the choice of Tougaloo for this speech was intentional, given its history in the Civil Rights movement, along with the Colom campaign’s emphasis on energizing college students across the state. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:25 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 The President of Tougaloo College is taking the stage now. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:25 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 The program is officially starting. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:21 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Colom’s family and friends are slowly making their way to their seats. Someone has passed out American flags that a few in the crowd are waving. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:16 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 The sign on the lectern reads “Picked Another Senator.” It’s a reference to a spot for Colom that became known as the “pick another protein” ad. It went viral after Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, asked to address rising beef prices, admonished voters that they “have so many proteins to choose from.” (We interviewed the guy whose delivery of “I’d rather pick another senator” helped the ad go viral.) 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 9:04 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 We expect Scott Colom to speak shortly at Tougaloo College, after winning his Senate election. It is a poignant moment for so many here, especially give the historic nature of his win and the legacy of the college as a haven and proving ground for civil rights leaders and Black officials. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 8:40 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Scott Colom has arrived at Tougaloo College and just stepped into the campus chapel, to cheers and applause. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 8:30 p.m. ET Michael Goldberg Politics reporter for Mississippi Today, reporting from Jackson. 
 Amid exuberant celebrations by Democrats, Gov. Tate Reeves, a Republican, has offered his congratulations to Colom in a statement on social media. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 8:20 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Students are welcoming people to Tougaloo College, steps from the historic chapel where civil rights leaders spoke, with a dance tunnel. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 8:19 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Outside the historic chapel at Tougaloo College, it’s standing room only — all seats have been taken as people from across the city come to celebrate Scott Colom’s win. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 8:18 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 In recent days, students and Black leaders have gathered here for community and to receive updates about the lengthy effort to count votes. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 8:17 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Tougaloo College is a private, historically Black college just outside Jackson. It was known as a haven for civil rights organizers during the movement. The civil-rights leaders including Fannie Lou Hamer and Medgar Evers spoke at its chapel. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:48 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 The mood at Tougaloo College, a historically Black college that had served as a safe haven for civil rights leaders and activists, was exuberant. People were dancing to music, embracing and declaring, “Thank the Lord, we did it.” 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:46 p.m. ET Michael Goldberg Politics reporter for Mississippi Today, reporting from Jackson. 
 Terry Rogers II, 21, a senior studying political science at the historically Black Tougaloo College, spent Tuesday driving students in a college van between government offices to check on their ballots as the race remained uncalled. A day later, he was scrolling CNN when he saw the network called the race for Colom. He and a friend took a moment to cry … 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:43 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said Scott Colom’s win in the Mississippi Senate race proves that Southern Democrats are resurging … 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:25 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 When President Donald Trump refused to accept the results of the 2020 presidential election, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith was among a handful of senators who backed him up, voting to reject the results in Pennsylvania and Arizona in the early hours of Jan. 7, after Congress had reconvened in the aftermath of the attack on the Capitol the day before. Six years later, in her own election, she is conceding to a narrow loss. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:16 p.m. ET Theodore Schleifer 
 There has been a lot of commentary after last week’s results about whether big donors can actually swing races. Sometimes, they can. Consider Steve Pajcic, a surprise Democratic donor who emerged in mid-October to spend at least $7 million to back four red-state Democratic Senate candidates . Those races were all long shots then. But with Colom’s victory tonight, three of them have now won. The fourth, Angie Nixon in Florida, came awfully close. That’s an enviable track record. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:09 p.m. ET Michael Goldberg Politics reporter for Mississippi Today, reporting from Jackson. 
 At a bar in downtown Jackson, Robert Morris, 37, sat on the patio and said the U.S. Senate election made history he never expected to witness as a lifelong resident of the Deep South … 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:07 p.m. ET Theodore Schleifer 
 The Mississippi Senate race was one of the few where Democrats actually outspent Republicans on advertising. It was a relatively cheap battle, all told, with only about $22 million seen on the airwaves — but about 62 percent of that favored Colom over Hyde-Smith. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:07 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in Congress, was first appointed to the Senate to fill a vacancy in April 2018. She had previously served as Mississippi’s commissioner of agriculture from 2012 to 2018. She also spent more than a decade in the State Senate, starting as a conservative Democrat in 2000 and converting to the Republican Party in 2010. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:03 p.m. ET Emily Cochrane Reporting from Jackson, Miss. 
 Scott Colom will be the third Black senator ever to represent Mississippi. The first two were chosen by the state legislature and served during Reconstruction. Colom will be the first Black senator chosen by voters. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 7:02 p.m. ET Shane Goldmacher 
 The victory of Scott Colom means that at least 55 senators will be aligned with the Democratic Party next year, with the race in Alaska still uncalled. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:54 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Mississippi Republican, conceded in a video posted to social media on Wednesday evening … 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:50 p.m. ET Jennifer Medina 
 Derrick Johnson, the national president of the N.A.A.C.P., said in a statement that “Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out.” This year, the N.A.A.C.P. opened 11 field offices and registered more than 17,000 voters, he said. “Even in the face of efforts to remove voters from the rolls, attempts to intimidate voters and election officials, and bids to create fear around the electoral process, Mississippi voters showed up. They showed up for their communities, for their families, and for the future of their state. They reminded the nation that we the people have the power.” 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:48 p.m. ET Theodore Schleifer 
 Many will be able to claim some credit for the victory of Scott Colom. Among them are George and Alex Soros. The liberal mega-donors have been supporters of Colom since at least 2015, when the family donated about $900,000 to a PAC supporting Colom’s successful run for district attorney. The younger Soros hosted a fundraiser last year at his New York home for Colom, then very much a long-shot candidate. And a super PAC that spent for Colom, Fulcrum, received most of its money, $1 million, from the Soros family’s super PAC. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:44 p.m. ET Campbell Robertson 
 In post on social media, Randall Woodfin, the mayor of Birmingham, Ala., who is also a Black Democrat, congratulated Mr. Colom. “They said the South will rise again,” he wrote, “but they never said which South.” 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:41 p.m. ET Michael Goldberg Politics reporter for Mississippi Today, reporting from Jackson. 
 Representative Justis Gibbs, a Democratic state lawmaker, was at his Jackson law office when the race was called for Colom, who will become the first Black senator from Mississippi in nearly 150 years. Everyone stopped working and screamed for joy, he said … 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:37 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 Before this week, no Democrat had won Mississippi’s Senate race since 1982, when Senator John C. Stennis won a seventh term. As a staunch segregationist, Stennis had been a member of an earlier iteration of the Democratic Party. He renounced those views toward the end of his career, in the early 1980s. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:32 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 Scott Colom is currently leading Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 4,669 votes with around 99% of ballots counted, according to The Associated Press. His margin could change slightly, but the call means that The A.P. does not see a path to victory for Hyde-Smith. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:31 p.m. ET Jennifer Medina 
 With the election of Colom, there will now be seven Black senators next year, the highest number in history. In addition to Colom, Julianna Stratton, the senator-elect from Illinois, will join Senators Angela Alsobrooks, Cory Booker, Lisa Blunt Rochester, Tim Scott and Raphael Warnock. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:28 p.m. ET Campbell Robertson 
 U.S. Representative Bennie Thompson, until today Mississippi’s sole Black congressman, congratulated Colom in a statement, saying that his campaign “brought together Mississippians from every walk of life — young and old, black and white, rural and urban — in a way I have never witnessed in more than 50 years of public service.” 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:28 p.m. ET Jennifer Medina 
 Senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat from California, connected Colom’s win to voting rights. “Just a few thousand votes made the difference,” the former California secretary of state wrote in a post on X. “Never let anyone tell you your vote doesn’t matter. That’s why they keep trying to go after our right to vote. When the people turn out, justice wins.” 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:20 p.m. ET Michael Kruse 
 Wilbur Colom, Scott Colom’s father, told The New York Times Wednesday that Hyde-Smith had gotten in touch with Colom’s team to concede the race. 
 Nov. 11, 2026, 6:06 p.m. ET Bayliss Wagner 
 Senator Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Senate Democratic campaign arm, congratulated Senator-elect Scott Colom for breaking the party’s more than 40-year drought in Mississippi Senate races on Wednesday evening … 
 Nov. 6, 2026, 6:53 p.m. ET John Yoon 
 Nancy Lacore, a Democratic former Navy admiral who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, flipped the South Carolina House seat held by Representative Nancy Mace, a Republican who ran unsuccessfully for governor instead of seeking re-election, according to The Associated Press … 
 Nov. 6, 2026, 5:34 p.m. ET Tim Balk 
 Eliott Rodriguez, a South Florida Democrat whose race for the House remains too close to call , filed a lawsuit on Friday in federal court in Miami requesting that the Miami-Dade County elections supervisor, Alina Garcia, recuse herself from any recount process in his race … 
 Nov. 6, 2026, 4:27 p.m. ET Evan Reynolds Election data reporter 
 In the Mississippi Senate race, Scott Colom’s lead over Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, grew to about 2,500 votes on Friday, according to The Associated Press, after three more counties reported votes around 4:10 p.m. Eastern. Colom’s margin has increased by nearly 700 votes today, though just under 1,500 new votes have been reported statewide. 
 Nov. 6, 2026, 4:18 p.m. ET Christine Zhang 
 The next batches of votes from Alaska are expected to be posted on Monday and Tuesday, according to the state’s Division of Elections. These are expected to consist of ballots cast early in-person and by mail … 
 Nov. 6, 2026, 3:49 p.m. ET Lauren McGaughy Texas politics reporter 
 Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat who has served in the Texas House for more than 50 years, just announced in the Texas State Capitol that she had enough votes to become speaker next year. Thompson said she would work with Republicans, who are now in the minority party for the first time in more than 20 years, when state lawmakers meet for their next session in January. “I do not have a dictatorship,” she said … 
 Nov. 6, 2026, 3:12 p.m. ET Lauren McGaughy Texas politics reporter 
 In the Texas Capitol today, Senfronia Thompson, who has been in the State House since 1973, will announce she has more than enough support to become speaker. The Texas House press room is packed with lawmakers, staff members and members of the news media awaiting the announcement … 
 Nov. 6, 2026, 2:11 p.m. ET David Chen National reporter 
 Arizona Democrats have won the State Senate and State House of Representatives, according to The Associated Press. Coupled with Gov. Katie Hobbs’s re-election victory, Democrats will now have a trifecta — both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — for the first time since the mid-1960s. In fact, the Democrats have not had an outright majority in any legislative chamber in Arizona since the early 1990s.

 Sources: Election results and race calls are from The Associated Press. The Times publishes its own estimates for each candidate’s share of the final vote and the number of remaining votes, based on historic turnout data and reporting from results providers. These are only estimates, and they may not be informed by reports from election officials. County type designations are based on a New York Times analysis of data from the U.S. Census, the National Center for Health Statistics, and other research. County and township demographics, including median household income, race/ethnicity, age and educational attainment, are from the census. Age shares represent a percentage of the adult population, and college-educated shares represent a percentage of adults age 25 and older. High-income refers to a median household income of $100,000 and higher.
